AA Breakdown Cover for Motorbikes: Everything You Need to Know

I'll be straight with you – breaking down on a bike is a different beast to breaking down in a car. I've been there: sat on the verge of the A9 near Pitlochry with a dead battery, watching the Scottish rain roll in. That's when you really appreciate proper breakdown cover.

The AA has been the go-to for British motorists for decades, but how does their breakdown service actually stack up for us bikers? I've used them myself, I've spoken to other riders who swear by them, and I've done the research so you don't have to. Let me walk you through everything you need to know about AA breakdown cover for motorbikes in 2026.

Why Breakdown Cover Matters for Motorcycle Tourers

Look, I get it. We all like to think our bikes are bulletproof. But I've seen BMWs fail in the Highlands, Triumphs give up on the NC500, and even Honda reliability legends refuse to start in a Snowdonia car park. It happens.

The thing about bikes is that when they break down, you're more vulnerable than car drivers. You can't just sit inside out of the weather. You can't pile all your gear into the recovery vehicle as easily. And if you're touring – especially somewhere remote like the Scottish islands – you need to know someone's coming to get you.

I learned this the hard way on the B4391 in Wales. Beautiful road, middle of nowhere, and my clutch cable snapped. No phone signal, rain coming in, and the nearest town was Bala – about twelve miles away. That's when I realised breakdown cover isn't just insurance; it's peace of mind.

What AA Motorcycle Breakdown Cover Actually Includes

The AA offers several tiers of cover, and they all work for motorbikes. Here's what you're actually getting:

Roadside Assistance

This is the basic level. If you break down more than a quarter-mile from home, they'll come out and try to fix you at the roadside. I've had AA patrols sort out everything from flat batteries to loose connections while I stood there in my gear. The patrols carry a decent toolkit and know their way around most common bike issues.

What I like is that they understand bikes. The patrol who helped me near Applecross knew exactly where to check on my Yamaha. He had me running again in twenty minutes. Not all breakdown services have that bike-specific knowledge.

At Home Cover

This extends coverage to your home address. Sounds unnecessary until you're trying to get to the ferry terminal at Oban for an island tour and your bike won't start on your driveway. Been there. The AA came out, sorted the issue, and I made my ferry with ten minutes to spare.

National Recovery

This is where it gets serious for touring riders. If the patrol can't fix you at the roadside, they'll recover you, your bike, and your pillion to a destination of your choice anywhere in the UK. When my gearbox decided it had enough near Keswick, they took me and my Tiger all the way back to Bristol. That's over 300 miles. In a car recovery service, that would've cost me hundreds of pounds.

Onward Travel

If you're more than 25 miles from home when you break down, the AA will sort you out with onward travel. That could be a hire vehicle, hotel accommodation, or train tickets. For touring, this is essential. When I broke down in Fort William, they put me up in a hotel overnight while they arranged recovery to a local mechanic the next morning.

European Cover

Planning to take the bike across the Channel? The AA offers European breakdown cover too. I used it last year in France and it worked seamlessly. Same standard of service, just with local contractors who actually turned up faster than I expected.

How Much Does AA Breakdown Cover Cost for Bikes?

Right, let's talk money. As of 2026, AA motorcycle breakdown cover starts around £7-8 per month for basic roadside assistance. That's cheaper than a pint in most biker cafés.

If you want the full works – roadside, home, national recovery, and onward travel – you're looking at roughly £12-15 per month. For serious touring riders, this is the package I recommend. When you're planning multi-day routes using VisorUp's route builder, the last thing you want is to worry about recovery costs if something goes wrong.

The AA often runs promotions, especially at the start of riding season. I've seen new members get their first year at significant discounts. Keep an eye out around March and April.

Here's my take: if you're doing any touring beyond day trips, comprehensive AA breakdown cover pays for itself the first time you use it. One recovery from the Scottish Highlands could easily cost £500-800 without cover.

What Actually Happens When You Break Down

Let me walk you through the process from experience:

First, you call the AA breakdown number or use their app. The app is brilliant – it uses GPS to pinpoint your exact location, which is crucial when you're on some unnamed B-road in the Peak District with no idea what to tell them.

They'll ask you what's wrong, what bike you're riding, and whether you're in a safe location. If you're not safe – say you've broken down in a live lane or on a blind corner – they'll prioritise you. I've had 20-minute response times when I've been in dodgy positions.

The patrol arrives, assesses the situation, and either fixes you there or arranges recovery. With bikes, they use specialist motorcycle trailers or recovery trucks with proper securing equipment. Your bike won't just be thrown in the back of a van.

If you're touring with luggage, they'll make sure everything goes with you. I had a full set of Kriega panniers and camping gear when I broke down on the A537 (Cat and Fiddle). Everything came with me in the recovery vehicle.

AA Breakdown vs Other Providers for Bikers

I've tried a few breakdown services over the years. Here's how the AA compares:

AA vs RAC

Both are solid for bikes. The RAC is slightly cheaper in some packages, but I've found AA has better rural coverage. When you're touring in Wales or Scotland, that matters. The RAC is excellent if you're mostly riding in urban and suburban areas.

AA vs GEM

GEM is the bike-specific option, and they're brilliant. Genuinely excellent service tailored for motorcyclists. They're often a bit more expensive, but every recovery vehicle is bike-equipped. If you're riding something specialist – a classic, a sports bike, or an adventure bike with loads of kit – GEM might be worth the extra.

AA vs Bennetts

Bennetts partners with the AA for their breakdown cover anyway, so you're getting AA service through Bennetts branding. Sometimes Bennetts offers better bundle deals if you're getting insurance through them too.

Specific Considerations for Touring Riders

If you're using VisorUp to plan serious tours, here's what you need to think about with breakdown cover:

Remote Coverage

The NC500, the Welsh mountains, the Yorkshire Dales – these are where breakdowns hurt most. The AA has good coverage in remote areas, but response times can still be 90+ minutes. I've waited two hours on the A93 near Glenshee. Bring a book, a flask, and proper weatherproof gear.

Make sure your touring kit includes layers and waterproofs that'll keep you comfortable during a wait. I've stood in Scottish rain for an hour waiting for recovery – trust me, cheap rain gear doesn't cut it. Check out SportsBikeShop for proper all-weather riding gear that'll keep you dry and warm during those roadside waits.

Multi-Day Tours

If you break down on day two of a week-long Scottish tour, onward travel becomes crucial. The AA's higher tier packages will get you to your next accommodation or help you arrange alternative transport. I broke down once near Ullapool – the AA got my bike to a local garage and me to my hotel. The garage fixed it overnight, and I was back on the road the next afternoon.

Ferry and Island Coverage

Planning to ride to Skye, Mull, or the Western Isles? Breakdown cover works, but recovery logistics get complicated. The AA will recover you to the nearest ferry terminal or arrange local service, but getting your bike off an island might take a day or two. Factor this into your touring schedule.

What AA Breakdown Cover Doesn't Include

Be realistic about the limits:

  • Running out of fuel: They'll help you out, but you might get charged. Carry a reserve and know your bike's range.
  • Crash damage recovery: If you've had an accident, that's an insurance matter, not breakdown cover. Different process entirely.
  • Off-road recovery: If you've taken your adventure bike properly off-road and got stuck, standard breakdown cover might not help. Check your policy.
  • Modifications and non-standard bikes: Heavily modified bikes or very rare models might need specialist recovery. Declare modifications when you sign up.
  • Repeat breakdowns: If you keep calling them out for the same fault, they'll expect you to get it properly fixed. Fair enough, really.

Tips from Real-World Touring Experience

After years of using breakdown services while touring across Britain, here's my practical advice:

Save the breakdown number in your phone properly: Not just in contacts, but somewhere you can access even if your phone is playing up. I keep it written on a card in my tank bag too.

Know your bike's details: Registration, make, model, colour. Sounds obvious, but when you're stressed and wet, you might blank on basic info.

Carry basic tools anyway: Breakdown cover is for when you can't fix it. But a loose bolt or a simple adjustment? Sort it yourself and keep moving. I carry a basic toolkit that's saved me multiple times.

Take photos of where you break down: The GPS on your phone isn't always accurate. A photo of a landmark or road sign helps the patrol find you faster, especially on rural routes.

Be honest about the problem: If you've run out of fuel, say so. If you've crashed, say so. The patrol needs to know what they're dealing with.

Check your cover before big tours: I review my breakdown cover every spring before planning summer tours. Make sure it's current and covers what you need.

The Bottom Line on AA Breakdown for Bikers

Look, I'm not on commission here. I'm just a rider who's broken down enough times to know that proper breakdown cover is non-negotiable. The AA works well for motorcycles, has decent coverage across Britain, and won't leave you stranded on the side of the A9 wondering how you'll get home.

Is it perfect? No. Response times in remote areas can be slow. You're still going to have a frustrating wait sometimes. But compared to paying hundreds of pounds for a single recovery, or trying to sort out your own logistics when you're broken down in the Lakes, it's worth every penny.

For touring riders especially – those of us planning routes through the best British roads, heading up to Scotland, or spending long weekends in Wales – comprehensive AA breakdown cover is as essential as good tyres and proper gear. Get sorted before you ride out, and you'll have one less thing to worry about when you're carving through the Highlands or exploring the best motorcycle roads the UK has to offer.

Get Yourself Covered

Here's what I'd do: go to the AA website, get a quote for the comprehensive package (roadside, home, recovery, and onward travel), and set it up before your next tour. It takes ten minutes. Then use VisorUp's trip planner to map out your next adventure knowing that if the worst happens, you're covered.

Ride safe, plan smart, and I'll see you out there on the roads.
